title: Half of all neutron stars may be born as magnetars
freshness: Published in Nature Astronomy on 10 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: A new study suggests that roughly half of the dense stellar remnants called neutron stars may be born as magnetars — objects with extraordinarily powerful magnetic fields. That would make these extreme stars much more common than astronomers previously estimated.
whyItMatters: Magnetars may be far more common than astronomers thought. If roughly half of neutron stars are born with these extraordinarily powerful magnetic fields, magnetars could be a much more important source of the Universe’s brightest explosions and mysterious radio flashes than previous estimates suggested.

body:
## Half, from a population model, not from a headcount

A Nature Astronomy paper published on 10 September 2026 concludes that magnetars may be about half of all neutron stars at birth. The work was led by Celsa Pardo Araujo and Nanda Rea, with co-authors Ronchi and Graber, at the Institute of Space Studies of Catalonia and the Institute of Space Sciences in Barcelona. It is a population synthesis: a simulation of how neutron stars evolve from the supernova that makes them to the objects we catalog now. It is not a new survey that classified half the neutron stars in the Milky Way one by one.

Neutron stars are what some massive stars leave behind. In the Milky Way, the IEEC account says, there are on the order of a hundred billion stars, and about one percent of them — roughly a hundred million — are neutron stars. Magnetars are the subset with exceptionally strong magnetic fields. They have been treated as rare. Rare made it awkward to blame them for the rates of superluminous supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and fast radio bursts, all of which need a powerful central engine often enough that a scarce magnetar population struggles to keep up.

## One model for objects that used to be filed separately

Earlier tallies tended to treat radio pulsars, magnetars, central compact objects, and X-ray isolated neutron stars as separate boxes. There are evolutionary links between those boxes. A magnetar can spin down, its field can decay, and it can spend part of its life looking like something else. If you ignore the links, you mis-count the birth fraction.

This paper puts the main types of isolated neutron stars into one framework. It folds in how they are distributed in the galaxy, how they spin down, how they cool, how their fields evolve, and the biases of the observations that find them. From that, the authors infer both the magnetar fraction and the supernova rate the Milky Way needs.

The rate part is a check, not a footnote. Core-collapse supernovae from stars of roughly 8 to 25 solar masses are what produce these remnants. To match the neutron stars we actually detect, the models need more than two such explosions per century in the observed population. The team gets a rate two ways: from supernova remnants, and from the neutron-star counts. With that rate in hand, the birth fraction that fits is around 50 percent. Pardo Araujo’s conclusion is that magnetars would then be common enough to power a significant share of those bright transients.

## What “around 50 percent” is allowed to do

It is an average from a model that reproduces galactic observations. Change the field-decay law, or the beaming, or the supernova rate, and the percentage can move. The paper’s claim is that a large fraction is no longer an exotic extra. It is what the unified model prefers. Previous studies that assumed magnetars were rare were using a narrower bookkeeping.

Rea points at the obvious next test: other galaxies. The same synthesis could predict a magnetar population, then compare it with the observed rates of superluminous supernovae, fast radio bursts, and gamma-ray bursts outside the Milky Way. That comparison needs each galaxy’s star-formation history, because the supernova rate will not match ours. Until that is done, the 50 percent is a Milky Way inference.

The Nature Astronomy article is the authority for the model and the fraction. The IEEC note is a clear secondary account. Neither is a catalogue of new magnetars. If you want the observational counterparts, they are still the galactic pulsars and the transient surveys. This paper is about whether those counterparts can be the same objects seen at different ages, born common rather than rare.
